`ggplot2` is not a menu of chart types. It is a grammar: you say what data to
use, which variable maps to which visual property, and what shape to draw. Three
decisions, three pieces of code.

## The three pieces

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

survey <- tibble(
  id       = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
  age      = c(23,45,67,34,56,29,71,38,52,41,60,33,48,25,63,55,30,44,58,36),
  sbp      = c(112,138,162,124,145,118,171,129,150,133,158,121,142,115,160,148,120,136,155,127),
  district = c("Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur",
               "Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar",
               "Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur"),
  smoker   = c(FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,
               TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,
               FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE)
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point()
```

Read it in three parts:

| Part | Says |
|---|---|
| `ggplot(survey, ...)` | use this dataset |
| `aes(x = age, y = sbp)` | put age on the x axis, blood pressure on y |
| `geom_point()` | draw each row as a point |

`aes()` is short for *aesthetic mapping*: it connects a column in your data to
something you can see. `geom_` functions say what shape to draw.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Layers join with `+`, not `|>`
This is the one place in the tidyverse where the pipe does not apply.
`ggplot2` is older than the pipe and uses `+` to add layers. Using `|>` here
gives an error that does not explain itself.
:::

## Mapping a third variable

Anything inside `aes()` is driven by the data. Map `smoker` to colour and
ggplot2 splits the points and builds a legend for you:

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
survey <- tibble(
  age = c(23,45,67,34,56,29,71,38,52,41,60,33,48,25,63,55,30,44,58,36),
  sbp = c(112,138,162,124,145,118,171,129,150,133,158,121,142,115,160,148,120,136,155,127),
  smoker = c(FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE)
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

Note where `size = 3` went: **outside** `aes()`. That is the rule, and it is
easy to get wrong the first time.

- Inside `aes()` — "this property comes from a column".
- Outside `aes()` — "this property is a fixed setting for the whole layer".

`colour = smoker` inside means colour by the smoking column. `colour = "blue"`
outside would mean make every point blue.

## Distributions: the histogram

One variable, so only `x`. A histogram counts how many observations fall in each
bin.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
survey <- tibble(
  sbp = c(112,138,162,124,145,118,171,129,150,133,158,121,142,115,160,148,120,136,155,127)
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, colour = "white")
```

Change `binwidth` to 5, then to 25, and run it again. The data has not changed;
the story has. Always say what binwidth you used.

## Comparing groups: the boxplot

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
survey <- tibble(
  sbp = c(112,138,162,124,145,118,171,129,150,133,158,121,142,115,160,148,120,136,155,127),
  district = c("Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur")
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = district, y = sbp)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## A boxplot of 7 points looks as confident as one of 600
Each box here rests on 6 or 7 observations. A box drawn over that few points
looks as authoritative as one drawn over 600. Add the points on top so the
reader can see how thin the evidence is:

```r
ggplot(survey, aes(x = district, y = sbp)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6)
```
:::

## Counting categories: the bar chart

`geom_bar()` counts rows for you. Give it only an `x`.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
survey <- tibble(
  district = c("Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur"),
  smoker = c(FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE)
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = district, fill = smoker)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

If you already have the counts in a column, use `geom_col()` instead, which
draws the number you give it rather than counting rows.

## Summarise first, then plot

Most real plots are not drawn from the raw rows. You summarise with the Primer 4
verbs, then pipe the result into `ggplot()`.

Note the join in the middle: `|>` between the dplyr steps, then `+` between the
ggplot layers. That switch is the whole trick.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

survey <- tibble(
  district = c("Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur",
               "Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar",
               "Tumkur","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur"),
  smoker   = c(FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,
               TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE)
)

survey |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    n_smokers   = sum(smoker),
    pct_smokers = round(mean(smoker) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = district, y = pct_smokers)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "District", y = "Smokers (%)")
```

`geom_col()` here, not `geom_bar()`: you have already worked out the number, so
you want it drawn, not counted again.

Add `filter(n >= 7)` as a line after `summarise()` and run it again. Hassan
disappears, because only 6 people there were surveyed. The pipeline is a list of
steps, so you can insert one anywhere.

It has to go **after** `summarise()`, because that is the step that creates the
`n` column. Put it before and R will tell you `n` does not exist.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why summarise before plotting
A bar chart of raw rows can only ever show counts. The moment you want a
percentage, a mean, a rate or a risk on the y axis, you have to compute it
first. That is why `dplyr` and `ggplot2` are taught together.
:::

## Labels are not decoration

A plot that needs you standing next to it is not finished. `labs()` is the
cheapest improvement you can make to one.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
survey <- tibble(
  age = c(23,45,67,34,56,29,71,38,52,41,60,33,48,25,63,55,30,44,58,36),
  sbp = c(112,138,162,124,145,118,171,129,150,133,158,121,142,115,160,148,120,136,155,127),
  smoker = c(FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,TRUE,TRUE,FALSE)
)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "Systolic blood pressure rises with age in this sample",
    subtitle = "20 adults screened in three districts, 2026",
    x        = "Age (years)",
    y        = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
    colour   = "Current smoker",
    caption  = "Simulated data for teaching."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Two habits worth copying from that cell:

1. The title says what the reader should **conclude**, not what the axes are.
   "Systolic blood pressure rises with age" beats "Scatter plot of SBP by age".
2. The caption says the data is simulated. If your data is real, the caption is
   where the source goes.

## What you should now be able to do

- Build a plot from data, an `aes()` mapping, and a `geom_`.
- Tell when something goes inside `aes()` (it comes from a column) and when it
  goes outside (it is a fixed setting).
- Draw a scatter plot, a histogram, a boxplot and a bar chart.
- Add layers with `+`, not `|>`.
- Label a plot so it survives being separated from you.
